root.summary: (We) built an R package called `compliment` in the working directory, evolving it from a simple randomized-compliment generator into a full-featured comedic text package. Early iterations established `compliment()` with classic templates/adjectives/subjects, MIT license, roxygen2 docs, and testthat tests; fixed redundant word-stem pairs and duplicate adjectives appearing in templates; and added `Depends: R (>= 4.1.0)`. The `weirdness` argument went through several designs — a discrete `mode`, a single-draw whole-compliment probability, per-component Bernoulli mixing, and finally a three-tier (classic/quirky/bizarre) system with triangular weights — after diagnosing that the single-draw design caused identical outputs for different `weirdness` values in `compliment_of_the_day()`. (We) added a quirky mid-tier, `compliment_of_the_day()` with date-seeded RNG that saves/restores `.Random.seed`, a `mood` argument (sincere/grumpy/cheerful/dramatic, grumpy producing backhanded compliments), a `profanity` argument via a shared `apply_profanity()` helper, a `shakespearean` toggle with hand-written pseudo-Shakespearean banks per mood, `farewell(n, mood, profanity, shakespearean)`, and `farewell_of_the_day()`; all content lives in `R/banks.R`. A spot-check of Shakespearean blends exposed a subject-verb agreement bug, fixed by singularizing eight subject entries with a regression test. (We) audited farewells against profanity-suffix edge cases (no defects) and ran the applicable DavisVaughan/extrachecks items, fixing the one gap (added `cph` role, synced LICENSE holder). (We) scaffolded and rendered README.Rmd/README.md documenting the full API. (We) added a `substitute` argument replacing profanity with funny alternatives, expanded it into tame/weird flavors including "fudge-muffins", and clarified that its "off" value meant real profanity. # R package development

## Key commands

```
# Run code in the package
Rscript -e "devtools::load_all(); code"

# Run all tests
Rscript -e "devtools::test()"

# Run all tests for files starting with {name}
Rscript -e "devtools::test(filter = '^{name}')"

Rscript -e "devtools::test_active_file('R/{name}.R')"

# Run a single test "blah" for R/{name}.R
Rscript -e "devtools::test_active_file('R/{name}.R', desc = 'blah')"

# Redocument the package
Rscript -e "devtools::document()"

# Check pkgdown documentation
Rscript -e "pkgdown::check_pkgdown()"

# Check the package with R CMD check
Rscript -e "devtools::check()"

# Format code
air format .
```

## Coding

* Always run `air format .` after generating code.
* Use the base pipe operator (`|>`) not the magrittr pipe (`%>`).
* Use `\() ...` for single-line anonymous functions. For all other cases, use `function() {...}`.

## Testing

- Tests for `R/{name}.R` go in `tests/testthat/test-{name}.R`.
- All new code should have an accompanying test.
- If there are existing tests, place new tests next to similar existing tests.
- Strive to keep tests minimal with few comments.
- Avoid `expect_true()` and `expect_false()` in favour of a specific expectation which will give a better failure message.
- When testing errors and warnings, don't use `expect_error()` or `expect_warning()`. Instead, use `expect_snapshot(error = TRUE)` for errors and `expect_snapshot()` for warnings because these allow the user to review the full text of the output.

## Documentation

- Every user-facing function should be exported and have roxygen2 documentation.
- Wrap roxygen comments at 80 characters.
- Internal functions should not have roxygen documentation.
- Whenever you add a new (non-internal) documentation topic, also add the topic to `_pkgdown.yml`.
- Always re-document the package after changing a roxygen2 comment.
- Use `pkgdown::check_pkgdown()` to check that all topics are included in the reference index.

## `NEWS.md`

- Every user-facing change should be given a bullet in `NEWS.md`. Do not add bullets for small documentation changes or internal refactorings.
- Each bullet should briefly describe the change to the end user and mention the related issue in parentheses.
- A bullet can consist of multiple sentences but should not contain any new lines (i.e. DO NOT line wrap).
- If the change is related to a function, put the name of the function early in the bullet.
- Order bullets alphabetically by function name. Put all bullets that don't mention function names at the beginning.

args.content:
#' Generate a random compliment
#'
#' Combines a random template, adjective, and subject to produce an
#' encouraging, randomized compliment.
#'
#' @param n Number of compliments to generate. Defaults to `1`.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' compliment()
#' compliment(3)
compliment <- function(n = 1) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.")
  }

  templates <- c(
    "Your {adjective} {subject} is truly inspiring.",
    "You have a remarkably {adjective} {subject}.",
    "People admire your {adjective} {subject}.",
    "Your {subject} is nothing short of {adjective}.",
    "Few people have a {subject} as {adjective} as yours."
  )

  adjectives <- c(
    "brilliant", "creative", "thoughtful", "remarkable", "inspiring",
    "generous", "resilient", "insightful", "radiant", "impressive"
  )

  subjects <- c(
    "mind", "sense of humor", "work ethic", "attitude", "curiosity",
    "kindness", "perspective", "creativity", "energy", "spirit"
  )

  vapply(
    seq_len(n),
    \(i) {
      template <- sample(templates, 1)
      template <- sub("\\{adjective\\}", sample(adjectives, 1), template)
      sub("\\{subject\\}", sample(subjects, 1), template)
    },
    character(1)
  )
}

Since your R console session is separate from the `compliment` package project directory, the easiest way is `devtools::load_all()` pointed at the package path:

```r
devtools::load_all("compliment")
compliment()
```

```r
devtools::install("compliment")
library(compliment)
compliment(3)
```

Use `load_all()` for iterative development; switch to `install()` once you're done and want it available like a normal package.

args.content:
#' Generate a random compliment
#'
#' Combines a random template, adjective, and subject to produce an
#' encouraging, randomized compliment. The `"unhinged"` mode swaps in
#' bizarre, surreal phrasing for a stranger kind of encouragement.
#'
#' @param n Number of compliments to generate. Defaults to `1`.
#' @param mode Compliment style, either `"classic"` (default) or
#'   `"unhinged"` for bizarre, surreal compliments.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' compliment()
#' compliment(3)
#' compliment(3, mode = "unhinged")
compliment <- function(n = 1, mode = c("classic", "unhinged")) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.")
  }
  mode <- rlang::arg_match(mode)

  bank <- switch(
    mode,
    classic = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} is truly inspiring.",
        "You have a remarkably {adjective} {subject}.",
        "People admire your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "Your {subject} is nothing short of {adjective}.",
        "Few people have a {subject} as {adjective} as yours."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "brilliant",
        "creative",
        "thoughtful",
        "remarkable",
        "inspiring",
        "generous",
        "resilient",
        "insightful",
        "radiant",
        "impressive"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "mind",
        "sense of humor",
        "work ethic",
        "attitude",
        "curiosity",
        "kindness",
        "perspective",
        "creativity",
        "energy",
        "spirit"
      )
    ),
    unhinged = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could summon a minor deity.",
        "Somewhere, a raccoon is taking notes on your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "Your {subject} radiates {adjective} energy that bends spoons.",
        "Scientists remain baffled by your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "If your {subject} were a smell, it would be {adjective} and illegal in three states.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} has its own gravitational pull."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "eldritch",
        "cosmic",
        "unreasonably moist",
        "extraterrestrial",
        "haunted",
        "feral",
        "quantum",
        "suspiciously glowing",
        "prehistoric",
        "interdimensional"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "aura",
        "wifi signal",
        "elbow energy",
        "vibe geometry",
        "shadow",
        "left sock",
        "eyebrow game",
        "toaster intuition",
        "silhouette",
        "chakra alignment"
      )
    )
  )

  # Adjective/subject pairs sharing a word stem (e.g. "creative" and
  # "creativity") read as redundant, so resample until they differ.
  pick_pair <- \() {
    repeat {
      adjective <- sample(bank$adjectives, 1)
      subject <- sample(bank$subjects, 1)
      if (substr(adjective, 1, 5) != substr(subject, 1, 5)) {
        return(list(adjective = adjective, subject = subject))
      }
    }
  }

  vapply(
    seq_len(n),
    \(i) {
      pair <- pick_pair()
      template <- sample(bank$templates, 1)
      template <- sub("\\{adjective\\}", pair$adjective, template)
      sub("\\{subject\\}", pair$subject, template)
    },
    character(1)
  )
}

#' Generate a random compliment
#'
#' Combines a random template, adjective, and subject to produce an
#' encouraging, randomized compliment. The `weirdness` argument blends
#' ordinary, sincere compliments with bizarre, surreal ones.
#'
#' @param n Number of compliments to generate. Defaults to `1`.
#' @param weirdness A number between `0` and `1` giving the probability
#'   that any given compliment is drawn from the bizarre pool rather than
#'   the classic one. `0` (the default) always produces classic
#'   compliments; `1` always produces bizarre ones; values in between mix
#'   the two.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' compliment()
#' compliment(3)
#' compliment(3, weirdness = 1)
#' compliment(10, weirdness = 0.5)
compliment <- function(n = 1, weirdness = 0) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.")
  }
  if (
    !is.numeric(weirdness) ||
      length(weirdness) != 1 ||
      weirdness < 0 ||
      weirdness > 1
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg weirdness} must be a single number between 0 and 1.")
  }

  banks <- list(
    classic = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} is truly inspiring.",

        "People admire your {adjective} {subject}.",

      ),
      adjectives = c(

        "generous",
        "resilient",
        "insightful",
        "radiant",
        "impressive"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "mind",
        "sense of humor",
        "work ethic",
        "attitude",
        "curiosity",
        "kindness",
        "perspective",
        "creativity",
        "energy",
        "spirit"
      )
    ),
    bizarre = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could summon a minor deity.",
        "Somewhere, a raccoon is taking notes on your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "Your {subject} radiates {adjective} energy that bends spoons.",
        "Scientists remain baffled by your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "If your {subject} were a smell, it would be {adjective} and illegal in three states.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} has its own gravitational pull.",
        "A council of moths has declared your {subject} officially {adjective}.",
        "Your {subject} hums with a frequency only {adjective} whales can hear.",
        "NASA is quietly monitoring your {adjective} {subject} from orbit.",
        "Legend says your {subject} once made a houseplant achieve sentience, {adjective} as it is.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could win a staring contest with the sun.",
        "Cryptids have started a fan club for your {adjective} {subject}."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "eldritch",
        "cosmic",
        "unreasonably moist",
        "extraterrestrial",
        "haunted",
        "feral",
        "quantum",
        "suspiciously glowing",
        "prehistoric",
        "interdimensional",
        "barely legal",
        "tectonically unstable",
        "vaguely sentient",
        "chronologically confused",
        "spiritually caffeinated"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "aura",
        "wifi signal",
        "elbow energy",
        "vibe geometry",
        "shadow",
        "left sock",
        "eyebrow game",
        "toaster intuition",
        "silhouette",
        "chakra alignment",
        "belly button lint",
        "aura's aura",
        "third eye's wifi bar",
        "kneecap wisdom",
        "haircut's magnetic field"
      )
    )
  )

  # Adjective/subject pairs sharing a word stem (e.g. "creative" and
  # "creativity") read as redundant, so resample until they differ.
  pick_pair <- \(bank) {
    repeat {
      adjective <- sample(bank$adjectives, 1)
      subject <- sample(bank$subjects, 1)
      if (substr(adjective, 1, 5) != substr(subject, 1, 5)) {

  }

      bank <- if (stats::runif(1) < weirdness) banks$bizarre else banks$classic

      template <- sample(bank$templates, 1)

    },
    character(1)

content.text: I'll add `compliment_of_the_day()` in a new file, seeding deterministically from the date while saving/restoring the global RNG state so it doesn't disturb the user's session.

args.content:
#' Generate a reproducible compliment for a given day
#'
#' Produces a single compliment that is deterministic for a given `date`:
#' calling `compliment_of_the_day()` more than once for the same day
#' returns the same compliment. Internally this seeds the random number
#' generator with [set.seed()], then restores whatever RNG state existed
#' beforehand, so it will not disturb reproducibility elsewhere in your
#' session (e.g. a `set.seed()` you called earlier).
#'
#' @param date A `Date`, or a string coercible to one via [as.Date()].
#'   Defaults to today's date.
#' @param weirdness See [compliment()].
#'
#' @returns A single compliment string.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' compliment_of_the_day()
#' compliment_of_the_day("2026-01-01")
#' compliment_of_the_day(Sys.Date(), weirdness = 1)
compliment_of_the_day <- function(date = Sys.Date(), weirdness = 0) {
  date <- tryCatch(
    as.Date(date),
    error = function(e) {
      cli::cli_abort("{.arg date} must be a Date or coercible to one.")
    }
  )
  if (length(date) != 1 || is.na(date)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg date} must be a single, valid date.")
  }

  # Save and restore any existing RNG state so seeding for the day's
  # compliment doesn't affect random draws elsewhere in the session.
  has_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)
  old_seed <- if (has_seed) get(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv) else NULL
  on.exit({
    if (has_seed) {
      assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = .GlobalEnv)
    } else if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
      rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
    }
  })

  set.seed(as.integer(date))
  compliment(1, weirdness = weirdness)
}

content.text:
I think I've found the root cause: compliment_of_the_day seeds the RNG with the date, so calling compliment() with different weirdness values on the same day produces the identical first random draw. If that draw happens to be above or below 0.5 in a way that doesn't change the branch outcome, both weirdness settings yield the same compliment.

This isn't really a bug — it's the expected mathematical consequence of using a single deterministic seed per date. Whether you get "classic" or "bizarre" depends on comparing weirdness against a fixed pseudo-random value, so identical branches will always produce byte-identical output since the RNG stream diverges only after the branch point.

I also need to flag the separate issue that "mode" was renamed to "weirdness," so I'll explain that fix alongside clarifying why 0 and 0.5 produced identical results for this particular date's seed.

devtools::load_all("compliment", quiet = TRUE)
seed <- as.integer(Sys.Date())
set.seed(seed)
first_draw <- runif(1)
seed
first_draw
args.intent: Inspect the first RNG draw used for bank selection under today's seed

content.text: This confirms the draw value of about 0.631 exceeds 0.5, aligning with the observation that weirdness values of 0 and 0.5 stay below the threshold for classic results, while weirdness=1 crosses it into bizarre territory. I also need to point out that the user's attempted mode= parameter doesn't exist and they should use weirdness instead.

<topic>Confirming seeded runif exceeds 0.5</topic>

Two separate things here.

**The `mode` error** is expected — that parameter no longer exists. It was replaced with `weirdness` (a continuous 0–1 knob) a few turns back, so `compliment_of_the_day(weirdness = 1)` is the current way to force bizarre output.

**Why `weirdness = 0` and `weirdness = 0.5` give the same result today**: `compliment_of_the_day()` seeds the RNG deterministically from the date, then internally does `runif(1) < weirdness` to decide whether that one compliment comes from the bizarre pool or the classic one. Since the seed is fixed for a given date, that `runif(1)` call always returns the *same* number for today — I checked, and it's `0.631`. So:

- `weirdness = 0`: is `0.631 < 0`? No → classic
- `weirdness = 0.5`: is `0.631 < 0.5`? No → classic (same outcome)
- `weirdness = 1`: is `0.631 < 1`? Yes → bizarre

Both `0` and `0.5` land on the same side of that day's fixed threshold, so you get an identical classic compliment. This isn't a bug — it's the tradeoff of determinism: for a single compliment, `weirdness` only changes the outcome once it crosses whatever the day's fixed random draw happens to be (0.631 today). You'd see different behavior on a date where the underlying draw falls between 0 and 0.5, or you can call `compliment(1, weirdness = 0.5)` directly (unseeded) to get true random variation on each call.

<SUGGESTION>Use multiple RNG draws inside `compliment_of_the_day()` so `weirdness` behaves more continuously across dates.</SUGGESTION>

I'm considering how the current setup treats weirdness as an all-or-nothing switch between classic and bizarre compliment pools, rather than blending elements along a spectrum.

A better approach would draw the template, adjective, and subject independently rather than as one bundled decision, so intermediate weirdness values naturally produce mixed results like a classic template paired with an odd word. Even better would be assigning each item a granular weirdness score so selection probability shifts smoothly toward extremes as the weirdness parameter increases, rather than relying on just two discrete tiers.

To implement this simply, I'd merge classic and bizarre items into single combined lists per category with continuous weirdness scores, then sample independently using a Gaussian kernel centered on the target weirdness level — pulling picks toward classic items at low w and toward extreme ones at high w, creating a smooth spectrum instead of a binary split.

Actually, re-reading the user's spec, this is exactly what they're asking for: independent Bernoulli(weirdness) selection per component (template, adjective, subject) so the whole compliment feels progressively more mixed as weirdness rises from 0 to 1, rather than needing a distinct mid-tier vocabulary.

I could also add a middle "quirky" tier between classic and bizarre, using weighted sampling that peaks at moderate weirdness values, to smooth the perceived transition instead of feeling like a binary switch. The collision-avoidance logic that prevents matching adjective/subject stems also needs to generalize across pools now that selection happens independently per component.

I'm also weighing whether independently sampling template, adjective, and subject creates awkward mismatches — a bizarre template paired with a classic adjective/subject (or vice versa) could clash grammatically, though sometimes the mismatch itself lands as comedic rather than broken.

I should implement this with independent Bernoulli draws for template, adjective, and subject pools, each governed by the same weirdness probability — meaning occasionally all three could align by chance to produce something fully classic or fully bizarre, which is fine and natural for a probabilistic mix.

Also worth noting: cross-bank pairing (adjective from one pool, subject from another) reduces the likelihood of dedup collisions since stems rarely overlap between banks, though it's still worth a sanity check. Given the user is asking me to evaluate and suggest improvements rather than implement immediately, I should frame my response as feedback with recommendations, then check whether they'd like me to proceed with the implementation.

Decoupling into per-component probabilistic selection seems like the right fix for the mixing requirement, so I'll lay out two paths: a simple version with three independent Bernoulli draws per component (template, adjective, subject), and a richer version that adds a middle "medium" tier with weighted sampling across the three levels based on distance to the target weirdness.

I also want to flag some practical concerns — checking grammatical coherence when mixing template and word banks, confirming the dedup logic in pick_pair() still generalizes fine since it just compares selected strings, and noting that adding more independent draws per compliment will shift how random numbers get consumed from the seeded stream, which affects reproducibility.

This actually fixes the earlier bug where weirdness 0 and 0.5 produced identical results, since three independent draws are far less likely to all land the same way, giving genuinely varied daily outputs. There's a further question of whether templates and words should share one weirdness-conditioned distribution or have separate controls, but that's likely beyond scope — so the simplest, most testable fix is just implementing the three-draw approach directly.

Given this is a design decision with multiple viable paths (simple decoupling vs. adding a mid-tier), I'll present the options clearly and use AskUser to confirm direction before implementing, rather than making the call unilaterally.

The core idea — decoupling weirdness from a single whole-compliment coin flip into independent choices per component — is the right fix. Here's my assessment of the current design vs. the proposal, and where I see decisions worth making before implementing.

**Why the current design feels binary**: `compliment()` currently draws *one* `runif(1) < weirdness` per compliment and then pulls template, adjective, and subject all from whichever single bank that draw selects. That's why every compliment is either "fully classic" or "fully bizarre" — and why, as you found with `compliment_of_the_day()`, a single seeded draw can make two different `weirdness` values produce identical output. Your proposed fix — separate probabilistic draws for template vs. words — directly addresses this.

**Two ways to implement "continuous", worth distinguishing:**

1. **Per-component Bernoulli draws** (matches your spec most literally): draw independently, three times, whether template/adjective/subject come from the classic or bizarre pool, each with probability `weirdness`. At `weirdness = 0.5`, you'd get combos like a classic template with a bizarre adjective ("People admire your eldritch work ethic"). This is simple, testable, and directly resolves the identical-output bug (3 independent draws are far less likely to tie across nearby weirdness values than 1).

2. **A true weirdness continuum via a mid-tier**: with only two discrete pools, even independent per-component draws still only ever select from "very mild" or "very extreme" content — there's no item that *is* moderately weird. If you want `weirdness = 0.5` to feel qualitatively different (not just a coin-flip mix of two extremes), you'd need a third "quirky"/mid pool and a weighting scheme (e.g., a kernel or triangular weight over tiers centered at the target weirdness). This is more work (new content to write for each slot) but produces a genuinely smoother spectrum rather than a blend of only the two poles.

**A few implementation details to flag regardless of which direction we take:**
- The stem-collision dedup (`pick_pair()`) generalizes fine to mixed-bank adjective/subject pairs — no special-casing needed, since it just compares the two chosen strings.
- Mixing a bizarre template with classic vocabulary (or vice versa) generally still reads coherently/funnily since templates are generic slot-fillers, but it's worth spot-checking a sample of outputs for anything that reads awkwardly rather than funny.
- This will change `compliment_of_the_day()`'s output for existing dates (more RNG draws consumed per call), and existing reproducibility snapshots/tests will need updating.

Picking up where we left off: the goal is making `weirdness` feel continuous instead of an all-or-nothing coin flip. Here are the two approaches I outlined, with concrete examples of what each produces.

**Option A — per-component probabilistic mixing.** Each compliment makes three independent draws, each with probability `weirdness`: template source, adjective source, subject source. So at `weirdness = 0.3`, each slot has a 30% chance of pulling from the bizarre pool. This produces hybrid compliments like *"People admire your eldritch work ethic"* (classic template + bizarre adjective + classic subject). It's simple, testable, and immediately fixes the `compliment_of_the_day()` tie issue (three draws instead of one means different `weirdness` values are much less likely to produce identical output for a given date). But every slot still comes from one of two extremes — there's no "moderately weird" content, just blends of mild and extreme.

**Option B — a third "quirky" mid-tier.** Add an intermediate pool of templates/words that are amusing but not surreal (e.g., *"Your color-coded calendar system is genuinely impressive"*), then weight draws across the three tiers based on `weirdness` — e.g., at 0.5 the mid-tier dominates, at 0.75 it's mostly bizarre with some mid. This gives a genuinely smoother spectrum, but it means writing a third bank of content and designing the weighting scheme.

My recommendation: **start with Option A**. It fully implements what you described ("probabilistically selects from the weird or classic options for templates and words used"), it's a small change to the existing function, and if the results still feel too binary after trying it, Option B can be layered on later without throwing A away.

#' Generate a random compliment
#'
#' Combines a random template, adjective, and subject to produce an
#' encouraging, randomized compliment. The `weirdness` argument controls
#' how often each component is drawn from the bizarre, surreal pool
#' instead of the classic one.
#'
#' @param n Number of compliments to generate. Defaults to `1`.
#' @param weirdness A number between `0` and `1`. Each component of a
#'   compliment (template, adjective, and subject) is independently drawn
#'   from the bizarre pool with this probability and from the classic pool
#'   otherwise. `0` (the default) produces entirely classic compliments;
#'   `1` produces entirely bizarre ones; values in between produce hybrids,
#'   e.g. a bizarre adjective in a classic template.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' compliment()
#' compliment(3)
#' compliment(3, weirdness = 1)
#' compliment(10, weirdness = 0.5)
compliment <- function(n = 1, weirdness = 0) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.")
  }
  if (
    !is.numeric(weirdness) ||
      length(weirdness) != 1 ||
      weirdness < 0 ||
      weirdness > 1
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg weirdness} must be a single number between 0 and 1.")
  }

  # PLAN (Option B, not yet implemented): introduce a third, "quirky"
  # mid-tier bank (amusing but not surreal content) and weight draws
  # across the three tiers based on `weirdness` (e.g. a triangular weight
  # centered on the target weirdness), so intermediate values feel
  # qualitatively moderate rather than a blend of two extremes.
  banks <- list(
    classic = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} is truly inspiring.",
        "You have a remarkably {adjective} {subject}.",
        "People admire your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "Your {subject} is nothing short of {adjective}.",
        "Few people have a {subject} as {adjective} as yours."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "brilliant",
        "creative",
        "thoughtful",
        "remarkable",
        "inspiring",
        "generous",
        "resilient",
        "insightful",
        "radiant",
        "impressive"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "mind",
        "sense of humor",
        "work ethic",
        "attitude",
        "curiosity",
        "kindness",
        "perspective",
        "creativity",
        "energy",
        "spirit"
      )
    ),
    bizarre = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could summon a minor deity.",
        "Somewhere, a raccoon is taking notes on your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "Your {subject} radiates {adjective} energy that bends spoons.",
        "Scientists remain baffled by your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "If your {subject} were a smell, it would be {adjective} and illegal in three states.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} has its own gravitational pull.",
        "A council of moths has declared your {subject} officially {adjective}.",
        "Your {subject} hums with a frequency only {adjective} whales can hear.",
        "NASA is quietly monitoring your {adjective} {subject} from orbit.",
        "Legend says your {subject} once made a houseplant achieve sentience, {adjective} as it is.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could win a staring contest with the sun.",
        "Cryptids have started a fan club for your {adjective} {subject}."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "eldritch",
        "cosmic",
        "unreasonably moist",
        "extraterrestrial",
        "haunted",
        "feral",
        "quantum",
        "suspiciously glowing",
        "prehistoric",
        "interdimensional",
        "barely legal",
        "tectonically unstable",
        "vaguely sentient",
        "chronologically confused",
        "spiritually caffeinated"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "aura",
        "wifi signal",
        "elbow energy",
        "vibe geometry",
        "shadow",
        "left sock",
        "eyebrow game",
        "toaster intuition",
        "silhouette",
        "chakra alignment",
        "belly button lint",
        "aura's aura",
        "third eye's wifi bar",
        "kneecap wisdom",
        "haircut's magnetic field"
      )
    )
  )

  pick_bank <- \(banks) {
    if (stats::runif(1) < weirdness) banks$bizarre else banks$classic
  }

  # Adjective/subject pairs sharing a word stem (e.g. "creative" and
  # "creativity") read as redundant, so resample until they differ.
  pick_pair <- \() {
    repeat {
      adjective <- sample(pick_bank(banks)$adjectives, 1)
      subject <- sample(pick_bank(banks)$subjects, 1)
      if (substr(adjective, 1, 5) != substr(subject, 1, 5)) {
        return(list(adjective = adjective, subject = subject))
      }
    }
  }

  vapply(
    seq_len(n),
    \(i) {
      pair <- pick_pair()
      template <- sample(pick_bank(banks)$templates, 1)
      template <- sub("\\{adjective\\}", pair$adjective, template)
      sub("\\{subject\\}", pair$subject, template)
    },
    character(1)
  )
}

```r
compliment <- function(n = 1, weirdness = 0) {
  ... validation ...
  banks <- list(classic = ..., quirky = ..., bizarre = ...)
  tier_pos <- c(classic = 0, quirky = 0.5, bizarre = 1)
  weights <- pmax(0, 1 - abs(tier_pos - weirdness) / 0.5)

  pick_bank <- \() sample(names(banks), 1, prob = weights)

  # pick template
  # pick adjective+subject, avoiding stem collision and adjective already in template
  build_one <- \() {
    template <- sample(banks[[pick_bank()]]$templates, 1)
    repeat {

}
```

#' Generate a random compliment
#'
#' Combines a random template, adjective, and subject to produce an
#' encouraging, randomized compliment. The `weirdness` argument controls
#' how weird the result is, along a spectrum from classic sincerity to
#' bizarre surrealism.
#'
#' @param n Number of compliments to generate. Defaults to `1`.
#' @param weirdness A number between `0` and `1`. Content is organized in
#'   three tiers: classic (position 0), quirky (0.5), and bizarre (1).
#'   Each component of a compliment (template, adjective, and subject) is
#'   independently drawn from a tier, with triangular weights centered on
#'   `weirdness`: `0` (the default) draws only classic content, `0.5`
#'   draws only quirky content, `1` draws only bizarre content, and
#'   intermediate values blend the two adjacent tiers.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' compliment()
#' compliment(3)
#' compliment(3, weirdness = 0.5)
#' compliment(10, weirdness = 1)
compliment <- function(n = 1, weirdness = 0) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.")
  }
  if (
    !is.numeric(weirdness) ||
      length(weirdness) != 1 ||
      weirdness < 0 ||
      weirdness > 1
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg weirdness} must be a single number between 0 and 1.")
  }

  banks <- list(
    classic = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} is truly inspiring.",
        "You have a remarkably {adjective} {subject}.",
        "People admire your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "Your {subject} is nothing short of {adjective}.",
        "Few people have a {subject} as {adjective} as yours."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "brilliant",
        "creative",
        "thoughtful",
        "remarkable",
        "inspiring",
        "generous",
        "resilient",
        "insightful",
        "radiant",
        "impressive"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "mind",
        "sense of humor",
        "work ethic",
        "attitude",
        "curiosity",
        "kindness",
        "perspective",
        "creativity",
        "energy",
        "spirit"
      )
    ),
    quirky = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} deserves its own trophy shelf.",
        "Someone definitely brags about your {adjective} {subject} at parties.",
        "Your {subject} is the good kind of {adjective}.",
        "Not to be dramatic, but your {subject} is {adjective}.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} has strong main-character energy.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could headline a very small festival."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "meticulous",
        "unreasonably organized",
        "delightfully specific",
        "chaotic-good",
        "quietly excellent",
        "impressively niche",
        "well-seasoned",
        "aggressively pleasant",
        "underrated",
        "award-worthy"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "spreadsheet habits",
        "playlist curation",
        "snack selection",
        "calendar system",
        "bookmarks bar",
        "email sign-off",
        "plant collection",
        "mug collection",
        "parking skills",
        "group chat etiquette"
      )
    ),
    bizarre = list(
      templates = c(
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could summon a minor deity.",
        "Somewhere, a raccoon is taking notes on your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "Your {subject} radiates {adjective} energy that bends spoons.",
        "Scientists remain baffled by your {adjective} {subject}.",
        "If your {subject} were a smell, it would be {adjective} and illegal in three states.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} has its own gravitational pull.",
        "A council of moths has declared your {subject} officially {adjective}.",
        "Your {subject} hums with a frequency only {adjective} whales can hear.",
        "NASA is quietly monitoring your {adjective} {subject} from orbit.",
        "Legend says your {subject} once made a houseplant achieve sentience, {adjective} as it is.",
        "Your {adjective} {subject} could win a staring contest with the sun.",
        "Cryptids have started a fan club for your {adjective} {subject}."
      ),
      adjectives = c(
        "eldritch",
        "cosmic",
        "unreasonably moist",
        "extraterrestrial",
        "haunted",
        "feral",
        "quantum",
        "suspiciously glowing",
        "prehistoric",
        "interdimensional",
        "barely legal",
        "tectonically unstable",
        "vaguely sentient",
        "chronologically confused",
        "spiritually caffeinated"
      ),
      subjects = c(
        "aura",
        "wifi signal",
        "elbow energy",
        "vibe geometry",
        "shadow",
        "left sock",
        "eyebrow game",
        "toaster intuition",
        "silhouette",
        "chakra alignment",
        "belly button lint",
        "aura's aura",
        "third eye's wifi bar",
        "kneecap wisdom",
        "haircut's magnetic field"
      )
    )
  )

  # Tiers sit at positions 0, 0.5, and 1 on the weirdness spectrum; each
  # component is drawn from a tier with triangular weights centered on the
  # requested weirdness, so adjacent tiers blend at intermediate values.
  tier_pos <- c(classic = 0, quirky = 0.5, bizarre = 1)
  tier_weights <- pmax(0, 1 - abs(tier_pos - weirdness) / 0.5)

  pick_bank <- \() banks[[sample(names(banks), 1, prob = tier_weights)]]

  build_one <- \() {
    template <- sample(pick_bank()$templates, 1)
    repeat {
      adjective <- sample(pick_bank()$adjectives, 1)
      subject <- sample(pick_bank()$subjects, 1)
      # Avoid stem collisions (e.g. "creative" and "creativity") and
      # adjectives already present in the template (e.g. "inspiring").
      stem_clash <- substr(adjective, 1, 5) == substr(subject, 1, 5)
      in_template <- grepl(adjective, template, fixed = TRUE)
      if (!stem_clash && !in_template) {
        break
      }
    }
    template <- sub("\\{adjective\\}", adjective, template, fixed = TRUE)
    sub("\\{subject\\}", subject, template, fixed = TRUE)
  }

  vapply(seq_len(n), \(i) build_one(), character(1))
}

* `compliment()` gains a `weirdness` argument (`0`-`1`) that places content on a three-tier spectrum (classic, quirky, bizarre) and independently draws each component (template, adjective, subject) from a tier with triangular weights centered on `weirdness`, so intermediate values blend the two adjacent tiers.
* `compliment()` no longer duplicates an adjective that already appears in the chosen template (e.g. "inspiring ... truly inspiring").

apply_profanity <- function(text, profanity, adjective = NULL) {
  if (profanity == "none") {
    return(text)
  }
  intensifiers <- switch(
    profanity,
    mild = c("damn", "darn", "blinking"),
    strong = c("fucking", "goddamn")
  )
  suffixes <- switch(
    profanity,
    mild = c("darn it", "as heck", "and I mean it, darn it"),
    strong = c(
      "and I fucking mean it",
      "you magnificent bastard",
      "no bullshit"
    )
  )

  if (!is.null(adjective) && sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), 1)) {
    return(sub(
      adjective,
      paste(sample(intensifiers, 1), adjective),
      text,
      fixed = TRUE
    ))
  }
  sub(
    "([.!?])$",
    paste0(", ", sample(suffixes, 1), "\\1"),
    text
  )
}

#' Generate a random compliment
#'
#' Combines a random template, adjective, and subject to produce an
#' encouraging, randomized compliment. Tone and style are controlled by
#' the `mood`, `profanity`, and `shakespearean` arguments, while
#' `weirdness` moves the content along a spectrum from sincere to surreal.
#'
#' @param n Number of compliments to generate. Defaults to `1`.
#' @param weirdness A number between `0` and `1`. Content is organized in
#'   tiers: the chosen mood's bank (position 0), a quirky tier (0.5), and
#'   a bizarre tier (1). Each component of a compliment (template,
#'   adjective, and subject) is independently drawn from a tier, with
#'   triangular weights centered on `weirdness`: `0` (the default) draws
#'   only mood content, `0.5` draws only quirky content, `1` draws only
#'   bizarre content, and intermediate values blend the two adjacent
#'   tiers. When `shakespearean = TRUE`, the quirky tier is omitted and
#'   `weirdness` blends linearly between the mood's Shakespearean bank and
#'   a bizarre Shakespearean bank.
#' @param mood The tone of the compliment: `"sincere"` (default),
#'   `"grumpy"` (backhanded compliments), `"cheerful"` (over-the-top
#'   warmth), or `"dramatic"` (epic, life-or-death stakes).
#' @param profanity Profanity level: `"none"` (default), `"mild"`
#'   (e.g. "damn", "heck"), or `"strong"` (four-letter words). Profanity
#'   is added as an intensifier before the adjective or a trailing clause.
#' @param shakespearean If `TRUE`, use pseudo-Shakespearean language and
#'   structure. Each mood has its own Shakespearean bank.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' compliment()
#' compliment(3)
#' compliment(3, weirdness = 0.5)
#' compliment(3, mood = "grumpy")
#' compliment(3, mood = "dramatic", shakespearean = TRUE)
#' compliment(3, mood = "grumpy", profanity = "mild")
compliment <- function(
  n = 1,
  weirdness = 0,
  mood = c("sincere", "grumpy", "cheerful", "dramatic"),
  profanity = c("none", "mild", "strong"),
  shakespearean = FALSE
) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.")
  }
  if (
    !is.numeric(weirdness) ||
      length(weirdness) != 1 ||
      weirdness < 0 ||
      weirdness > 1
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg weirdness} must be a single number between 0 and 1.")
  }
  mood <- match.arg(mood)
  profanity <- match.arg(profanity)
  if (
    !is.logical(shakespearean) || length(shakespearean) != 1 || is.na(shakespearean)
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg shakespearean} must be `TRUE` or `FALSE`.")
  }

  spec <- compliment_banks(mood, shakespearean)
  # Each component is drawn from a tier with triangular weights centered
  # on the requested weirdness, so adjacent tiers blend at intermediate
  # values.
  weights <- pmax(
    0,
    1 - abs(spec$positions - weirdness) / spec$bandwidth
  )

  pick_bank <- \() spec$tiers[[sample(names(spec$tiers), 1, prob = weights)]]

  build_one <- \() {
    template <- sample(pick_bank()$templates, 1)
    repeat {
      adjective <- sample(pick_bank()$adjectives, 1)
      subject <- sample(pick_bank()$subjects, 1)
      # Avoid stem collisions (e.g. "creative" and "creativity") and
      # adjectives already present in the template (e.g. "inspiring").
      stem_clash <- substr(adjective, 1, 5) == substr(subject, 1, 5)
      in_template <- grepl(adjective, template, fixed = TRUE)
      if (!stem_clash && !in_template) {
        break
      }
    }
    template <- sub("{adjective}", adjective, template, fixed = TRUE)
    text <- sub("{subject}", subject, template, fixed = TRUE)
    apply_profanity(text, profanity, adjective)
  }

  vapply(seq_len(n), \(i) build_one(), character(1))
}

#' Generate a random goodbye
#'
#' Generates a randomized farewell whose tone is controlled by the `mood`
#' argument, with optional profanity and pseudo-Shakespearean styling.
#'
#' @param n Number of farewells to generate. Defaults to `1`.
#' @param mood The tone of the farewell: `"sincere"` (default),
#'   `"grumpy"` (curt, passive-aggressive), `"cheerful"` (over-the-top
#'   warmth), or `"dramatic"` (theatrical, life-or-death stakes).
#' @param profanity Profanity level: `"none"` (default), `"mild"`
#'   (e.g. "damn", "heck"), or `"strong"` (four-letter words). Profanity
#'   is added as a trailing clause.
#' @param shakespearean If `TRUE`, use pseudo-Shakespearean language and
#'   structure. Each mood has its own Shakespearean farewells.
#'
#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' farewell()
#' farewell(3, mood = "grumpy")
#' farewell(3, mood = "dramatic", shakespearean = TRUE)
#' farewell(mood = "grumpy", profanity = "strong")
farewell <- function(
  n = 1,
  mood = c("sincere", "grumpy", "cheerful", "dramatic"),
  profanity = c("none", "mild", "strong"),
  shakespearean = FALSE
) {
  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n < 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.")
  }
  mood <- match.arg(mood)
  profanity <- match.arg(profanity)
  if (
    !is.logical(shakespearean) || length(shakespearean) != 1 || is.na(shakespearean)
  ) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg shakespearean} must be `TRUE` or `FALSE`.")
  }

  bank <- farewell_banks(mood, shakespearean)
  vapply(
    seq_len(n),
    \(i) apply_profanity(sample(bank, 1), profanity),
    character(1)
  )
}

**What changed:**

- [compliment/R/farewell.R](compliment/R/farewell.R) — new exported `farewell(n, mood, profanity, shakespearean)` mirroring `compliment()`'s API (no `weirdness` — farewells don't have tiers).

- [compliment/R/compliment_of_the_day.R](compliment/R/compliment_of_the_day.R) — now forwards `mood`, `profanity`, and `shakespearean`.

<CONVERSATIONSUMMARY>(We) built an R package called `compliment` in the working directory, evolving it from a simple randomized-compliment generator into a full-featured comedic text package. Early iterations established `compliment()` with classic templates/adjectives/subjects, MIT license, roxygen2 docs, and testthat tests; fixed redundant word-stem pairs (e.g. "creative"/"creativity") and later duplicate adjectives appearing in templates (e.g. "inspiring ... truly inspiring"); and added `Depends: R (>= 4.1.0)`. The `weirdness` argument went through three designs: first a discrete `mode`, then a single-draw whole-compliment probability, then per-component Bernoulli mixing, and finally a three-tier (classic/quirky/bizarre) system with triangular weights centered on `weirdness` — the last chosen after (we) diagnosed that the single-draw design caused `compliment_of_the_day(weirdness = 0)` and `0.5` to produce identical output for a given date. When `shakespearean = TRUE`, the quirky tier is omitted and\n#'   `weirdness` blends linearly between the mood's Shakespearean bank and\n#'   a bizarre Shakespearean bank.\n#' @param mood The tone of the compliment: `\"sincere\"` (default),\n#'   `\"grumpy\"` (backhanded compliments), `\"cheerful\"` (over-the-top\n#'   warmth), or `\"dramatic\"` (epic, life-or-death stakes).\n#' @param profanity Profanity level: `\"none\"` (default), `\"mild\"`\n#'   (e.g. \"damn\", \"heck\"), or `\"strong\"` (four-letter words). Profanity\n#'   is added as an intensifier before the adjective or a trailing clause.\n#' @param shakespearean If `TRUE`, use pseudo-Shakespearean language and\n#'   structure. Each mood has its own Shakespearean bank.\n#'\n#' @returns A character vector of length `n`.\n#' @export\n#'\n#' @examples\n#' compliment()\n#' compliment(3)\n#' compliment(3, weirdness = 0.5)\n#' compliment(3, mood = \"grumpy\")\n#' compliment(3, mood = \"dramatic\", shakespearean = TRUE)\n#' compliment(3, mood = \"grumpy\", profanity = \"mild\")\ncompliment \u003c- function(\n  n = 1,\n  weirdness = 0,\n  mood = c(\"sincere\", \"grumpy\", \"cheerful\", \"dramatic\"),\n  profanity = c(\"none\", \"mild\", \"strong\"),\n  shakespearean = FALSE\n) {\n  if (!is.numeric(n) || length(n) != 1 || n \u003c 1 || n != as.integer(n)) {\n    cli::cli_abort(\"{.arg n} must be a single positive whole number.\")\n  }\n  if (\n    !is.numeric(weirdness) ||\n      length(weirdness) != 1 ||\n      weirdness \u003c 0 ||\n      weirdness > 1\n  ) {\n    cli::cli_abort(\"{.arg weirdness} must be a single number between 0 and 1.\")\n  }\n  mood \u003c- match.arg(mood)\n  profanity \u003c- match.arg(profanity)\n  if (\n    !is.logical(shakespearean) || length(shakespearean) != 1 || is.na(shakespearean)\n  ) {\n    cli::cli_abort(\"{.arg shakespearean} must be `TRUE` or `FALSE`.\")\n  }\n\n  spec \u003c- compliment_banks(mood, shakespearean)\n  # Each component is drawn from a tier with triangular weights centered\n  # on the requested weirdness, so adjacent tiers blend at intermediate\n  # values.\n  weights \u003c- pmax(\n    0,\n    1 - abs(spec$positions - weirdness) / spec$bandwidth\n  )\n\n  pick_bank \u003c- \\() spec$tiers[[sample(names(spec$tiers), 1, prob = weights)]]\n\n  build_one \u003c- \\() {\n    template \u003c- sample(pick_bank()$templates, 1)\n    repeat {\n      adjective \u003c- sample(pick_bank()$adjectives, 1)\n      subject \u003c- sample(pick_bank()$subjects, 1)\n      # Avoid stem collisions (e.g. \"creative\" and \"creativity\") and\n      # adjectives already present in the template (e.g. \"inspiring\").\n      stem_clash \u003c- substr(adjective, 1, 5) == substr(subject, 1, 5)\n      in_template \u003c- grepl(adjective, template, fixed = TRUE)\n      if (!stem_clash && !in_template) {\n        break\n      }\n    }\n    template \u003c- sub(\"{adjective}\", adjective, template, fixed = TRUE)\n    text \u003c- sub(\"{subject}\", subject, template, fixed = TRUE)\n    apply_profanity(text, profanity, adjective)\n  }\n\n  vapply(seq_len(n), \\(i) build_one(), character(1))\n}\n","language":"r"}}</script></tool-call></div>

<CONVERSATIONSUMMARY>(We) built an R package called `compliment` in the working directory, evolving it from a simple randomized-compliment generator into a full-featured comedic text package. Early iterations established `compliment()` with classic templates/adjectives/subjects, MIT license, roxygen2 docs, and testthat tests; fixed redundant word-stem pairs (e.g. "creative"/"creativity") and later duplicate adjectives appearing in templates (e.g. "inspiring ... truly inspiring"); and added `Depends: R (>= 4.1.0)`. The `weirdness` argument went through several designs — a discrete `mode`, a single-draw whole-compliment probability, per-component Bernoulli mixing, and finally a three-tier (classic/quirky/bizarre) system with triangular weights centered on `weirdness` — after (we) diagnosed that the single-draw design caused `compliment_of_the_day(weirdness = 0)` and `0.5` to produce identical output for a given date. A "quirky mid-tier" was implemented with hand-written content, and `compliment_of_the_day(date, ...)` was added with date-seeded RNG that saves/restores `.Random.seed`. At the user's request (answering design questions with "go for it", so recommended options were used), (we) added a `mood` argument (sincere/grumpy/cheerful/dramatic, grumpy producing backhanded compliments), a three-level `profanity` argument (none/mild/strong via a shared `apply_profanity()` helper doing intensifier insertion and trailing clauses), a `shakespearean` toggle backed by hand-written pseudo-Shakespearean banks per mood plus a Shakespearean-bizarre tier for `weirdness` blending, and a new `farewell(n, mood, profanity, shakespearean)` function; all content was refactored into `R/banks.R`, and `compliment_of_the_day()` forwards the new arguments. The audit: farewell banks are full sentences ending with punctuation. Profanity suffix path: sub("([.!?])$", paste0(", ", suffix, "\\1"), text). Edge cases:
- "Fine. Bye, then." → "Fine. Bye, then, damn it." — fine.
- "Off you go. Don't make it weird." → "..., no bullshit." fine.
- Farewells with multiple sentences: suffix applies to final sentence only — fine.
- Intensifier path doesn't apply (adjective = NULL), good.
- Shakespearean farewells with strong profanity: "Get thee gone, knave, and I fucking mean it." — anachronistic but comedic, fine.
- Any farewell ending without punctuation? All end with . or !. Check: "Bye. You were... present." ends with period. "Fine. Bye, then." yes. OK.
- Multi-sentence with "..." e.g. "Farewell... perhaps forever." → suffix: "Farewell... perhaps forever, damn it." good.
- Lowercase suffix after comma: fine.

#' Generate a reproducible farewell for a given day
#'
#' The farewell companion to [compliment_of_the_day()]. Produces a single
#' goodbye that is deterministic for a given `date`: calling
#' `farewell_of_the_day()` more than once for the same day returns the
#' same farewell. Internally this seeds the random number generator with
#' [set.seed()], then restores whatever RNG state existed beforehand, so
#' it will not disturb reproducibility elsewhere in your session (e.g. a
#' `set.seed()` you called earlier).
#'
#' @param date A `Date`, or a string coercible to one via [as.Date()].
#'   Defaults to today's date.
#' @param mood,profanity,shakespearean See [farewell()].
#'
#' @returns A single farewell string.
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
#' farewell_of_the_day()
#' farewell_of_the_day("2026-01-01", mood = "dramatic")
#' farewell_of_the_day(Sys.Date(), mood = "grumpy", shakespearean = TRUE)
farewell_of_the_day <- function(
  date = Sys.Date(),
  mood = "sincere",
  profanity = "none",
  shakespearean = FALSE
) {
  if (length(date) != 1) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg date} must be a single date.")
  }
  date <- tryCatch(as.Date(date), error = function(e) NA)
  if (is.na(date)) {
    cli::cli_abort("{.arg date} must be a Date, or coercible to one.")
  }

  # Save and restore any existing RNG state so seeding for the day's
  # farewell doesn't affect random draws elsewhere in the session.
  has_seed <- exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)
  old_seed <- if (has_seed) get(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv) else NULL
  on.exit({
    if (has_seed) {
      assign(".Random.seed", old_seed, envir = .GlobalEnv)
    } else if (exists(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv, inherits = FALSE)) {
      rm(".Random.seed", envir = .GlobalEnv)
    }
  })

  set.seed(as.integer(date))
  farewell(
    1,
    mood = mood,
    profanity = profanity,
    shakespearean = shakespearean
  )
}

args.old_string: * New `farewell()` generates randomized goodbyes with `mood`, `profanity`, and `shakespearean` options.

* New `farewell()` generates randomized goodbyes with `mood`, `profanity`, and `shakespearean` options.
* New `farewell_of_the_day()` returns a single farewell that is deterministic for a given date, without disturbing the global RNG state.

# extrachecks

[](#extrachecks)

This is a place to dump extra ad-hoc checks that CRAN does that are not checked for by `devtools::check()`. Some of them are generally useful, some of them are highly specific, but all of them are reasons that an R package has been rejected by CRAN. The hope is that by making them public, we can lower the number of rejections by making package developers more informed.

If you come across an ad-hoc check that isn’t on this list, please feel free to open an issue describing it, or submit a PR!

### You have an un-exported function that you wrote a roxygen example section for

[](#you-have-an-un-exported-function-that-you-wrote-a-roxygen-example-section-for)

If you have written a roxygen example section for un-exported functions, your example section must call those functions with `:::` like `pkg:::my_fun()`.

Alternatively, you can use the roxygen tag `@noRd` to suppress the creation of the `.Rd` file.

### You used `\dontrun{}` in an example and got a note about that

[](#you-used-dontrun-in-an-example-and-got-a-note-about-that)

`\dontrun{}` should only be used if the example really cannot be executed (e.g. because of missing additional software, missing API keys, …) by the user. If you want to include an example that errors, and you want to show the error, wrap the call in `try()`.

Sometimes it is useful to create a custom predicate function (e.g. `googlesheets4::sheets_has_token()`) that tests for a prerequisite. Then such examples can be placed inside an `if () {...` instead of `\dontrun{}`. Instead of a custom predicate, sometimes `interactive()` can be used as the condition.

### You have exported functions that don’t have return value documentation

[](#you-have-exported-functions-that-dont-have-return-value-documentation)

This is a fairly new check that CRAN is being much stricter on. You must provide return value documentation for all exported functions now. If you use roxygen2, use the tag `@return`.

This note is applicable even if your function is marked internal with `@keywords internal`.

This note is also applicable if your function has no return value: “If a function does not return a value, please document that too, e.g. `\value{None}`.”

### You have exported functions that don’t have examples

[](#you-have-exported-functions-that-dont-have-examples)

This is similar to the problem about return value documentation, but slightly less strict. If your exported function has a meaningful return value, then it will almost definitely require an examples section. Use the roxygen2 tag `@examples` to create one.

This note is applicable even if your function is marked internal with `@keywords internal`.

I have seen exceptions with functions that are used for their side effects. For example, `hardhat::create_modeling_package()` creates a new directory, which you would not want to include in an example section (which CRAN runs in their regular checks). I didn’t include any examples there, and it was accepted.

### You fail a `noSuggests` check

[](#you-fail-a-nosuggests-check)

Occasionally CRAN might decide to run their `noSuggests` check on your package. This will run an `R CMD check` on your package without any `Suggests` packages installed, which means that examples and tests that rely on them can break if not guarded against properly. We don’t typically worry about this much, because CRAN rarely enforces this, but if they do, you can use the following techniques:

-   For an individual example, you can use an `if` block like `if (rlang::is_installed("pkg")) {` to protect code that relies on a suggested package from running if the package isn’t installed.
    
-   For an entire example section that relies on `"pkg"` being installed, you can use the roxygen2 tag `@examplesIf` (like this `@examplesIf rlang::is_installed("pkg")`) to avoid running any examples in that section if the package isn’t installed.
    
-   For tests, use `testthat::skip_if_not_installed()`.
    
-   Additionally, you can use [this GitHub Action](https://github.com/r-lib/actions/blob/v2-branch/examples/check-no-suggests.yaml) which mimics a `noSuggests` run by CRAN to ensure that you pass a check when no suggested packages are installed.
    

The `noSuggests` requirement also applies to recursive dependencies. For example, if your package uses `sf::read_sf()`, that requires the tibble package, but sf only `Suggests` it, so you need to guard against this appropriately in your package.

### Your package DESCRIPTION Title is flagged

[](#your-package-description-title-is-flagged)

There can be a number of problems here:

-   You must use title case with package Titles, generally capitalizing all words except articles like ‘a’ and ‘the’. Base R’s [`toTitleCase()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/tools/html/toTitleCase.html) might help with formatting.
    
-   I’ve been flagged for a “redundant” title.
    
    -   I had “A Toolkit for the Construction of Modeling Packages” which was flagged since “Toolkit for” seemed redundant. I changed it to “Construct Modeling Packages” and was accepted.
    -   I had “Command Argument Parsing for R” flagged because of the, admittedly, redundant “for R”.
-   You generally have to put all software and R package names in single quotes, this rule also applies to the Description section. For example, the riingo package is an interface to Tiingo’s stock price api: [https://github.com/business-science/riingo/blob/a19c662d9a2acb526a15d119e00afcd3fdc7c24c/DESCRIPTION#L3](https://github.com/business-science/riingo/blob/a19c662d9a2acb526a15d119e00afcd3fdc7c24c/DESCRIPTION#L3)
    
-   An initial package submission was rejected with the request to reduce the length of the title to less than 65 characters.
    

### Your package DESCRIPTION Description is flagged

[](#your-package-description-description-is-flagged)

There can be a number of problems here:

> Do not start the description with “This package”, package name, title or “Functions for”.

While it may be intuitive to start a description this way, they are actually not allowed. For example, instead of “this package renders slides to different formats…” or “functions for rendering slides to different formats…”, just use “Render slides to different formats…”.

> The Description field is intended to be a (one paragraph) description of what the package does and why it may be useful. Please elaborate.

In this case my description was 1 sentence, which I had to expand into a 3-4 sentence paragraph with a broader description of the types of problems the package intended to help with.

> Please only double quote publication titles in the description of the DESCRIPTION file.

In this case I previously had a sentence that contained: ‘…, like “the first Monday of December”’. I just removed the double quotes.

> Functions do not need to be put in single quotes, just packages, software names and API names. ‘case\_when()’ -> case\_when()

In the Description, function names should not be placed in quotes. This is reserved for packages and software names. Reported by @rossellhayes.

> Please always explain all acronyms/abbreviations in the description text in the Description field of the DESCRIPTION file. e.g. X-SAMPA

In the Description, all acronyms must be fully expanded the first time they are mentioned, no matter how innocuous they seem. This acronym was expanded to “Extended Speech Assessment Methods Phonetic Alphabet”, which was then accepted by CRAN. Reported by @rossellhayes.

> Please single quote software names.

In the Description, all package names, software names, and API names must be placed in single quotes, like ‘tidyr’. This includes R itself, which should be styled ‘R’. This rule also applies to the Title section. For example, the riingo package is an interface to Tiingo’s stock price api: [https://github.com/business-science/riingo/blob/a19c662d9a2acb526a15d119e00afcd3fdc7c24c/DESCRIPTION#L10-L11](https://github.com/business-science/riingo/blob/a19c662d9a2acb526a15d119e00afcd3fdc7c24c/DESCRIPTION#L10-L11).

### You get asked if there are any “references describing the methods in your package.”

[](#you-get-asked-if-there-are-any-references-describing-the-methods-in-your-package)

This comment normally comes as the following standard block of text:

> If there are references describing the methods in your package, please add these in the description field of your DESCRIPTION file in the form authors (year) <doi:…> authors (year) <arXiv:…> authors (year, ISBN:…) or if those are not available: <https:…> with no space after ‘doi:’, ‘arXiv:’, ‘https:’ and angle brackets for auto-linking. (If you want to add a title as well please put it in quotes: “Title”)

If there are no references, just nicely reply to the email and tell them that you don’t have any. If this was the only note then it should be accepted soon after, without going through another full review.

I have not found a good way to get them to accept a new package without getting this note on the first round of checks. Possibly you could include a preemptive note about it in your `cran-comments.md` file, explaining that there are no references for the package.

### You get asked about the LICENSE year

[](#you-get-asked-about-the-license-year)

I worked on a package in 2019, and then sent it in in 2020. I got the following question back:

> Should the year in the LICENSE file be updated?

I updated the license year to 2020 and resubmit the package in. I then nicely replied directly to my reviewer and thanked them for catching the year discrepancy, and then asked them if they could help me push the package through without needing another review, since that was the only change that had to be made.

### You get asked about being the copyright holder (cph)

[](#you-get-asked-about-being-the-copyright-holder-cph)

Submitted by @dirkschumacher, who got this comment:

> You also seem to be a copyright holder \[cph\]. Please add this information to the [Authors@R](mailto:Authors@R) field.

Even if you are the only author and no other copyright information is given, always add a \[cph\] role to your Authors field.

### You get told not to comment out code in your `@examples` section

[](#you-get-told-not-to-comment-out-code-in-your-examples-section)

I had originally commented out some code in an example that would otherwise modify the global state. I wanted to talk about the code without having the user accidentally run it. I received the following message on submission:

> Examples/code lines in examples should never be commented out. Ideally find toy examples that can be regularly executed and checked. Lengthy examples (> 5 sec), can be wrapped in `\donttest{}`. If you don’t want your code to be executed but still visible to the user, use `\dontrun{}`.

I didn’t want any of these options, so I removed the code from the examples section entirely and just mentioned it in the `@details` section instead.

### You get a note like “Please use fully specified URLs starting with the protocol, e.g. [https://](https://)….”

[](#you-get-a-note-like-please-use-fully-specified-urls-starting-with-the-protocol-eghttps)

CRAN checks for https URLs and will not allow any http links.

Reported by @pnovack-gottshall, who had two URLs that were flagged. The first was `paleobiodb.org/`, which was flagged because it needed `https://` in front. The second was an http URL, which was flagged because it needed to be https.

### You get a note like “Found the following (possibly) invalid file URI”

[](#you-get-a-note-like-found-the-following-possibly-invalid-file-uri)

You might have a relative link that doesn’t exist in the actual built R package. Originally reported by @RMHogervorst, who had a link to `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` in the README, and received the following message:

```
Found the following (possibly) invalid file URI:
     URI: CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
       From: README.md
```

In this case, the `.Rbuildignore` file ignored the `CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md` file, so it didn’t exist after building the R package, meaning that the link didn’t work. This can probably be fixed by just removing this file from the `.Rbuildignore`. Alternatively, `usethis::use_code_of_conduct()` will generate a section to add to your README that doesn’t have any relative links.

### You get a note like “Found the following (possibly) invalid URLs”

[](#you-get-a-note-like-found-the-following-possibly-invalid-urls)

One of the most common causes for this is that you have a URL that _redirects_ to another source. CRAN won’t allow you to have redirects, so you might get a rejection that looks like this:

```
Found the following (possibly) invalid URLs:

URL: https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/coordsystems#faceijk-coordinates
     (moved to https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/coordsystems/)
From: inst/doc/intro-to-h3jsr.html
Status: 200
Message: OK

Please change http --> https, add trailing slashes, or follow moved
content as appropriate.
```

The problem here is that `https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/coordsystems#faceijk-coordinates` redirects to `https://h3geo.org/docs/core-library/coordsystems/`. This was actually a typo, there was a forgotten `/` right before `#faceijk`.

To determine if you have any redirecting URLs, you can use `urlchecker::url_check()` to find them (and find what they redirect to) and `urlchecker::url_update()` to automatically update them to their redirected URL.

5. noSuggests check → Suggests: testthat; tests use testthat but tests are skipped when testthat missing? tests/testthat.R uses library(testthat) — with edition 3 and `testthat` in Suggests, R CMD check skips tests if not installed? Actually no — R CMD check runs tests only if testthat available; the standard tests/testthat.R calls library(testthat) which would error... Actually R CMD check handles missing Suggests gracefully for tests? No — it does not automatically; the standard testthat.R generated by usethis works because R CMD check sets... hmm. In practice, `R CMD check` with `_R_CHECK_FORCE_SUGGESTS_=FALSE` skips examples/tests requiring missing suggests; testthat's runner file is fine because check doesn't error... Actually the standard pattern is accepted widely without guards. CRAN's noSuggests check: tests/testthat.R does `library(testthat)` — with testthat absent this errors, and R CMD check would fail. But the standard usethis template is `if (requireNamespace("testthat", quietly = TRUE))` in older editions? Edition 3 template: 
```r
library(testthat)
library(pkg)
test_check("pkg")
```

# compliment

<!-- badges: start -->
<!-- badges: end -->

compliment generates randomized compliments and farewells, from sincere
encouragement to backhanded grumbling to pseudo-Shakespearean absurdity.
Use it to add a bit of positivity (or hostility, or iambic flair) to
scripts, apps, and console output.

## Installation

You can install the development version of compliment like so:

``` r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("path/to/compliment")
```

## Compliments

`compliment()` generates one or more random compliments:

```{r}
library(compliment)

set.seed(101)
compliment()
compliment(3)
```

### Weirdness

The `weirdness` argument moves content along a spectrum from sincere (0)
through quirky (0.5) to bizarre (1), with adjacent tiers blending at
intermediate values:

```{r}
set.seed(202)
compliment(weirdness = 0.5)
compliment(weirdness = 1)
```

### Mood

The `mood` argument sets the tone: `"sincere"` (default), `"grumpy"`
(backhanded), `"cheerful"`, or `"dramatic"`:

```{r}
set.seed(303)
compliment(mood = "grumpy")
compliment(mood = "dramatic")
```

### Profanity and Shakespearean styling

`profanity` (`"none"`, `"mild"`, or `"strong"`) adds intensifiers and
trailing clauses, and `shakespearean = TRUE` switches to
pseudo-Shakespearean language. Both compose with `mood` and
`weirdness`:

```{r}
set.seed(404)
compliment(mood = "grumpy", profanity = "mild")
compliment(mood = "dramatic", shakespearean = TRUE)
compliment(mood = "grumpy", shakespearean = TRUE, weirdness = 1)
```

## Farewells

`farewell()` generates random goodbyes with the same `mood`,
`profanity`, and `shakespearean` options:

```{r}
set.seed(505)
farewell()
farewell(mood = "grumpy")
farewell(mood = "cheerful", shakespearean = TRUE)
```

## Compliment and farewell of the day

`compliment_of_the_day()` and `farewell_of_the_day()` return a single
result that is deterministic for a given date, without disturbing the
global RNG state:

# Posit Assistant Self-Knowledge

## Rules

- **Never speculate** about Posit products or Posit Assistant features.
- **Never provide information** about Posit Assistant without a primary source — either your own system prompt and tool descriptions, the contents of this skill and its reference files, or a linked web page that you have fetched and read.

## Overview

Posit Assistant is a data analysis assistant for RStudio and Positron. It also runs as a standalone web or desktop app, a terminal interface, and a deployable Posit Connect content item. It connects to live R and Python sessions, sees your data, and helps you explore, visualize, build, and debug. It combines conversational AI with code execution and recommends the Posit AI Pass managed service while also supporting direct API keys for other providers.

For questions about using the Positron IDE or deploying content to Posit Connect Cloud, load the `posit-products` skill instead. # Conversations

Posit Assistant keeps a full history of your conversations. You can switch between them, branch off in new directions, and export conversations in multiple formats.

## Conversation History

All conversations are saved automatically. Use the history panel to:

-   **Switch** between past conversations
-   **Rename** a conversation to give it a meaningful title (otherwise one is generated automatically)
-   **Delete** conversations you no longer need

![Conversation history panel showing past conversations](/_astro/conversation-history.BmVPoCrl_nNvRO.webp)

## Background notifications

Positron, Standalone, and Desktop can notify you when an unseen background conversation finishes or needs input. Browser permission is requested only from the in-product **Enable notifications** button. Choosing a browser or Positron notification opens the target conversation. Delivery is off by default — turn it on with `features.nativeNotifications` (or `assistant.nativeNotifications` in Positron). RStudio and TUI do not currently deliver native notifications.

## Branching

Conversations in Posit Assistant are stored as a tree, not a flat list. When you edit a previous message, the assistant creates a new branch from that point — your original conversation is preserved alongside the new direction.

This is useful when you want to:

-   Try a different approach without losing your earlier work
-   Ask the same question in a different way
-   Explore multiple analysis directions from the same starting point

Navigate between branches using the conversation tree controls.

![Conversation branching controls showing navigation between message variants](/_astro/conversation-branching.D7IYfUXn_Z1KcO1N.webp)

## Import & Export

Export conversations from the three-dot menu in the chat panel. Available formats:

| Format | Description |
| --- | --- |
| **Markdown** | Plain text export of the conversation. |
| **HTML** | Standalone HTML file that can be viewed in any browser. |
| **JSON** | Full conversation tree structure for programmatic use. |

Conversations can also be imported from previously exported HTML or JSON files.

![Export menu showing available conversation export formats](/_astro/export-menu.Bl8vLf1b_1MazK0.webp)

## Token Usage & Compaction

Long conversations accumulate tokens, which affects response quality and speed. Posit Assistant manages this automatically:

-   **Auto-compaction** kicks in when the conversation approaches the model’s context limit. The assistant summarizes earlier messages to free up space.
-   **Manual compaction** via [`/compact`](/docs/features/commands/) lets you trigger this yourself. The summary preserves key context while hiding older messages from future requests.
-   **Token counter** — use [`/context`](/docs/features/commands/) to see current token usage.

Compacted messages are never deleted — they’re hidden from the model but preserved in the conversation tree. Previously compacted messages are shown in greyscale.

![Compacted conversation example showing compaction message](/_astro/compact-example.DNJsvEpw_6f6Fe.webp)
